ta_reply:
That is exactly right, and the reasoning you just gave is the core insight. Well done.

This is actually the same guarantee you already rely on when you pass a variable by reference to a function. When you write `void foo(int &x)`, both the caller and `foo` are looking at the same memory location — there is only one `x`. A `[&ready]` capture works on precisely the same principle: the lambda does not get a snapshot copy, it holds a live alias to the original variable.

So when the notifying thread (the "setter") writes `ready = true`, and the waiting thread's predicate lambda (the "getter") evaluates `ready`, they are both reading and writing the same memory location — which is exactly what makes the synchronization meaningful.

This connects directly to a key property of `std::condition_variable`: the predicate is re-evaluated *after* each wakeup, so it is critical that the lambda sees the most up-to-date value of `ready`, not a stale copy taken at the moment the lambda was constructed. [1](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/lambda)
